hints: Think about what happens in a car engine when petrol burns to release heat energy, what reactant from air is always needed.
walkthrough:
Link fuel use to energy release**
When a hydrocarbon is used as a fuel you are burning it in air to release heat. Picture petrol vapour mixing with oxygen in the engine and igniting, that burning in oxygen has a special name you meet throughout AS chemistry.
Final answer: combustion

hints: Recall the two complete combustion products formed when a hydrocarbon containing only C and H burns in excess oxygen.
Start by balancing C to give $8\text{CO}_2$ and H to give $9\text{H}_2\text{O}$, then find the $\text{O}_2$ needed to supply all the O atoms.
walkthrough:
Write the skeleton with correct products**
Complete combustion of any hydrocarbon in excess oxygen gives only carbon dioxide and water. So start with $\ce{C8H18 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O}$.

Balance C and H first, then O**
$8$ C in octane needs $8\ce{CO2}$. $18$ H needs $9\ce{H2O}$. Count O on the right: $(8 \times 2) + (9 \times 1) = 25$ O atoms, so you need $25/2 = 12\frac{1}{2}$ $\ce{O2}$ on the left. That gives $\ce{C8H18 + 12 1/2 O2 -> 8CO2 + 9H2O}$.

hints: Think of the refinery process that breaks long chain alkanes into shorter alkanes for petrol plus alkenes for polymers.
walkthrough:
Connect low petrol supply to breaking long chains**
Crude oil contains too many long chain molecules and not enough short petrol sized molecules. Heating long alkanes strongly, often with a catalyst, splits them into shorter, more useful pieces. That breaking down process is called cracking.

hints: Recall that polymerisation of an alkene opens the $\text{C=C}$ double bond to form two new $\text{C-C}$ single bonds in a long chain.
Draw one $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)$ unit joined to a second $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)$ unit, with continuation bonds at each end and no double bond left.
walkthrough:
Open the double bond in your mind**
Take $\ce{CH3CH=CHCH3}$. In addition polymerisation the $\pi$ bond of $\ce{C=C}$ breaks and each C gains one new single bond to the next monomer. The two central C atoms each keep their $\ce{CH3}$ and H.

Draw one repeat unit with end bonds**
Draw $-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-$ with a short bond sticking out left and right to show continuation of the chain. Check every C has four single bonds, no $\ce{C=C}$ remains, and only one monomer unit is shown.
Final answer: Repeat unit: $-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-$ shown with extension bonds through each end C, single bonds only, each C bonded to one $\text{CH}_3$ and one H.

hints: Remember there are two polymer types, one from alkenes with no small molecule lost and one from monomers with two functional groups with a small molecule lost.
walkthrough:
Spot the monomer type**
But-2-ene is an alkene, $\ce{C=C}$, and the polymer forms by repeatedly adding across the double bond with nothing else lost. When the only product is the polymer itself, that is addition polymerisation.

hints: Think of the honeycomb device fitted in the exhaust system that uses Pt, Pd and Rh to convert CO and nitrogen oxides to harmless gases.
walkthrough:
Picture the exhaust clean up**
Hot exhaust gases pass over a metal honeycomb coated with platinum, palladium and rhodium. Those metals speed up redox reactions that turn CO, $\ce{NO_x}$ and unburnt hydrocarbons into $\ce{CO2}$, $\ce{N2}$ and water. That device is the catalytic converter.
Final answer: catalytic converter / catalyst

hints: Identify which gas is oxidised (CO to $\text{CO}_2$) and which is reduced ($\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{N}_2$) in the same equation.
walkthrough:
Pair oxidation with reduction**
CO picks up O to become $\ce{CO2}$, so it is oxidised. $\ce{NO2}$ loses O to become $\ce{N2}$, so it is reduced. Combine them so O atoms balance: $2\ce{CO} + \ce{NO2} -> 2\ce{CO2} + 1/2\ce{N2}$.
Final answer: $\ce{2CO + NO2 -> 2CO2 + 1/2 N2}$

hints: Recall the hazy, brownish pollution formed when unburnt hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides react in sunlight.
walkthrough:
Follow unburnt hydrocarbons in sunlight**
Unburnt hydrocarbons do not just disappear. In sunlight with nitrogen oxides they take part in complex reactions that build up ozone and a brownish haze over cities. That is photochemical smog, also accepted as fog, haze or global dimming.
Final answer: (photochemical) smog / fog / haze OR global dimming

hints: Think about what acid does to lakes, soil and living things, starting from lower pH harming fish and trees.
Think about what acid does to limestone buildings and how it dissolves aluminium compounds and nutrients from soil.
walkthrough:
Harm to water and life**
Acid rain lowers the pH of rivers and lakes and soil. That acidity kills fish, damages coral, and harms trees and crops.

Chemical leaching and material damage**
Acid dissolves toxic $\ce{Al^{3+}}$ from soil into water and washes out essential nutrients like $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$. It also attacks carbonate stone, so limestone buildings and statues are weathered and eroded.

Final answer: Any two from: lowers pH / increases acidity of rivers, lakes, oceans, soil; kills / harms fish, coral, plants, crops, trees; leaches toxic aluminium ions from soil into water; leaches away soil nutrients; damages / weathers / erodes buildings / statues.

hints: First consider how $\text{NO}_2$ can oxidise $\text{SO}_2$ by giving it an O atom, forming $\text{SO}_3$ and NO.
Then consider how the $\text{SO}_3$ formed reacts with rain water to give the acid rain acid $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$.
walkthrough:
Oxidise sulfur dioxide**
$\ce{NO2}$ acts as an oxidant, passing an O to $\ce{SO2}$: $\ce{NO2 + SO2 -> NO + SO3}$. Sulfur goes from +4 to +6.

Form the acid with water**
$\ce{SO3}$ is the anhydride of sulfuric acid and reacts readily with water in clouds: $\ce{SO3 + H2O -> H2SO4}$, which falls as acid rain.

Final answer: $\ce{NO2 + SO2 -> NO + SO3}$
$\ce{SO3 + H2O -> H2SO4}$

hints: Recall the key test for a catalyst, it is used up in one step but remade in a later step so overall amount is unchanged.
Look at the NO made in (d)(ii) and think how it can react with oxygen in air to remake the starting $\text{NO}_2$.
walkthrough:
Check the catalyst definition**
A catalyst speeds up reaction by a different route but is reformed unchanged at the end. Here $\ce{NO2}$ is consumed to make NO in $\ce{NO2 + SO2 -> NO + SO3}$, so for it to be catalytic that NO must be turned back into $\ce{NO2}$.

Write the regeneration step**
In air, NO is readily oxidised: $\ce{NO + 1/2 O2 -> NO2}$. Because $\ce{NO2}$ is remade, there is no net consumption, which is exactly why it is described as a catalyst.
Final answer: $\ce{NO2}$ is regenerated / not used up overall; $\ce{NO + 1/2 O2 -> NO2}$
